ordering_basis: Ordering is an editorial approximation of how commonly each food is eaten in the United States, informed by USDA per-capita availability categories. It is not a published ranking - no agency publishes one in this form - and small differences in position are not meaningful.
risk_basis: Risk is assigned by tier rather than per food, so two foods handled the same way cannot end up with different numbers. Foods that also appear in the detailed 16-food assessment use those figures directly.
key_point: Cyclospora is spread by fresh produce and water. It is not a meat, dairy, egg, grain or shelf-stable food pathogen, and cooking destroys it. Most of this list is negligible-risk for that reason, not because the risk is merely small.

raw-herb.basis: Raw leafy herbs. Crinkled leaf surfaces are close to a worst case for rinsing off oocysts, and herbs have a real U.S. outbreak history.

raw-leafy.basis: Raw leafy greens not implicated in 2026. Large folded surface area, eaten uncooked, and leafy greens have appeared in past outbreaks.

raw-soft.basis: Raw produce eaten whole and unpeeled, where the surface cannot be scrubbed hard. Washing helps only partially.

raw-firm.basis: Raw produce with a smooth firm surface that can be rinsed and rubbed, or an outer layer that is discarded.

peeled.basis: Peeled before eating. Contamination is a surface phenomenon, so removing the skin removes essentially all of it. Residual risk is knife cross-contamination from rind to flesh.

cooked-produce.basis: Produce that is essentially always cooked. Heating to about 158 F (70 C) inactivates Cyclospora, so the cooked food itself is not a route.

non-produce.basis: Not a produce item. Cyclospora is not a meat, dairy, egg, grain or shelf-stable food pathogen - it does not occur in these foods. Any residual risk comes from a raw produce garnish or from a shared cutting board.
